name: Retail
blurb: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation at volume, with NRF, Coresight, and IHL tracking the deployments.

points.desc: The Census BTOS series reports AI use for retail trade alongside every other sector, updated fortnightly.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

reading.body:
Retail AI is tracked by four independent sources covering adoption, store technology, market size, and software spend, but none of them measures the compute or power behind those systems.

The four sources form a layered measurement stack. Census BTOS updates adoption every two weeks across all sectors, including retail trade. NRF adds detail on store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software. Coresight sizes the market for merchandising and supply-chain logistics, while IHL tracks software expenditure and operational return in grocery, apparel, and general merchandise. Adoption is measured rather than guessed, and the Census series updates often enough to show change.

For AI specifically, the volume use cases are demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation. These run across many stores and transactions, so even small changes in adoption or software spend can signal where inference workloads are growing. But the data stops at adoption and spend. None of the four sources reports electricity demand, data center capacity, or compute requirements, so the data cannot support claims about grid constraints or building needs for retail AI.

summary: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation are the volume use cases.

analysis.body:
The Census BTOS series provides the measured adoption figure for retail trade, NAICS 44-45. Its latest reading shows 16.5% of retail firms answered yes when asked whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, up from 15.5% in the prior period. The series first asked the question in September 2023 and is updated fortnightly.

Per NRF, retail AI conversations now center on practical AI, connected stores, and relationship-driven loyalty, and NRF research covers store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software. IHL Group's page gives concrete deployment examples. Nature's Emporium uses Retailgrid's AI-powered spreadsheet and Price Radar platform to integrate daily sales data, model demand and price elasticity, and track four natural-products competitors plus Amazon.ca, starting with supplements. Rainbow's upgraded Shahe sp@ce supermarket in Shenzhen, built with Hanshow and Lingzhi Digital Technology, uses 17,000 IoT devices, NexConnect Smart Carts, Nebular Ultra ESLs, AI vision, robotics, and retail AI to improve navigation, fulfilment, shelf execution, and replenishment. Dr. Squatch uses AfterShip's AI-powered estimated delivery dates and AfterShip Intelligence on tracking pages to pair delivery visibility with personalized product recommendations.

Coresight Research is focused on scaling agentic AI in retail enterprises, with a presentation titled The IMPACT Playbook: How Retail Enterprises Scale Agentic AI hosted by Instacart at Groceryshop 2026. IHL Group's 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, in cooperation with Chain Store Age, finds that inventory data accuracy, not AI budget size, separates specialty retail winners from laggards. IHL also reports that most retail AI budgets fund the wrong layer first, and that inventory distortion is down to $1.7 trillion while empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion.

The clearest ROI evidence in the excerpts comes from Dr. Squatch, which achieved a 31.89% recommendation click-through rate, attributed $32,978 in Q1 revenue, cut WISMO inquiries 25%, and reached 94% delivery-date accuracy using AfterShip's tools. No other retail example in the source excerpts reports comparable return figures.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the sources point to a measured but still minority adoption level, 16.5% of retail firms, and to IHL's warning that budget size is less important than inventory data accuracy. The practical deployments highlighted by NRF and IHL concentrate on pricing, delivery visibility, store execution, and replenishment rather than broad agentic pilots.

https://nrf.com/.brief: The National Retail Federation describes itself as an advocate for the people, policies, and ideas that support a thriving retail sector, and it provides retail news, insights, and industry events. According to the organization, conversations held in Paris illustrated how retailers are putting what it calls "The Next Now" into practice. These efforts span practical artificial intelligence, connected stores, and loyalty programs built on relationships.

https://coresight.com/.brief: Coresight Research describes itself as a provider of data-based analysis focused on retail and technology, and says it has unique expertise in China within the industry. The page also states that the firm runs an exclusive, invite-only collaborative forum that examines AI opportunities and challenges for consumer-focused businesses. No market data or research findings are presented on this page.

https://ihlservices.com/.brief: IHL Group conducts research on retail technology spending and strategy. According to their 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, inventory data accuracy rather than AI budget size determines which specialty retailers succeed, and most retail AI budgets fund the wrong infrastructure layer first. The organisation also reports that inventory distortion has declined to $1.7 trillion, though empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion annually. IHL's analysis finds that the presence of AI does not predict pricing-platform quality among vendors, and retailers should instead evaluate explainability, automation controls, and governance safeguards.
